sections.title: Provider profiles construct clients; harness profiles shape agents
sections.body:
Provider and harness profiles are separate process-level configuration registries. Construction first resolves the model, then selects a harness; routing an individual request does not rerun the whole builder.

  1. Resolve provider construction settings. ProviderProfile supplies static kwargs, optional pre_init(spec), and an optional kwargs factory. Compose provider-wide and exact provider:model keys, with exact values taking precedence. Only the first colon separates provider/model. apply_provider_profile runs pre-init, combines static/factory settings, then lets explicit caller kwargs win.
  2. Account for merge phases. Hooks execute base then override, stopping on exceptions. Factories likewise run base then override, merging mappings with override keys winning. Factory output follows static kwargs, so a runtime default can supersede a static value: exact identity is not an unconditional winner across all phases.
  3. Select agent behavior. HarnessProfile controls base/suffix prompts, tool descriptions/exclusions, middleware exclusions/additions, and automatic general-purpose configuration. A prebuilt model bypasses provider construction defaults but still gets harness lookup. Original strings are used directly; otherwise lookup tries combined exact identity, a provider-qualified identifier exact key, then provider fallback. A bare identifier is not confused with an unrelated provider-wide key.

Lifetime: register before graph construction. These registries are not per-user authorization databases, and active-model routing does not automatically rebuild construction-time authored prompts or profile-selected stacks.

sections.title: Harness overlays use several identities and merge operations
sections.body:
Harness overlays use several merge identities. Read these as reference rules, not runtime execution steps.

  1. Merge fields by their own contract. Scalars use explicit non-None overrides; tool descriptions merge by tool name; excluded tool/middleware sets union. General-purpose fields merge individually, allowing an exact-model profile to re-enable a provider-disabled child or replace just its description. An explicit empty authored string can replace a base prompt; empty and None are not interchangeable.
  2. Distinguish middleware class from name. Profile extra_middleware merges by concrete class: replace existing class slots, append novel ones. Caller middleware= instead merges by .name; confusing these can add duplicates. Factories produce fresh instances per assembled stack. Static sequences reuse instances even though materialization returns a fresh list.
  3. Keep serializable configuration constrained. HarnessProfileConfig omits runtime-only extra_middleware and stores exclusions as names, not arbitrary import paths. Tests reject unknown keys and extra_middleware. Stable public serialized class aliases can round-trip; arbitrary class paths are not a hidden plugin loader.
  4. Match description keys exactly. Preserve {available_agents} in a task description override if specialists should remain visible. Stale tool-description keys silently do nothing. A correctly registered profile can still miss behavior because identity or tool names do not match the constructed surface.

sections.title: Built-ins, plugins and import-time costs
sections.body:
Built-ins and plugins initialize lazily on first registry access; importing the profiles package alone does not bootstrap them. Keep imports, client construction, graph caching, and provider prompt caches conceptually separate.

  1. Load registrations once. Bootstrap installs NVIDIA, OpenAI, and OpenRouter provider defaults plus model harness profiles, then discovers deepagents.provider_profiles and deepagents.harness_profiles entry points. A condition variable lets one thread initialize while others wait; same-thread registration-hook re-entry returns without deadlock.
  2. Handle failures by ownership. Built-in failures propagate and restore pre-bootstrap registry snapshots. Third-party failures log/warn and are isolated. Plugin order follows Python package metadata, and later additive registrations layer on earlier ones; do not rely on unrelated plugins deterministically owning the same key.
  3. Check exact model matches. anthropic:claude-sonnet-4-6 registers a suffix for parallel tools, investigating before answering, and reflecting on results. This is not evidence that every Anthropic model gets it or that a universal authored base prompt still exists.
  4. Treat prompt caching as provider integration. Anthropic caching delegates lazily only for request ChatAnthropic; Bedrock/Fireworks depend on installed modules and ignore unsupported models. Provider behavior and matching rendered prefixes—especially forks—still determine reuse, not an SDK cache-hit guarantee.

sections.title: Exclusions are guarded configuration, not a security perimeter
sections.body:
Exclusions are guarded configuration and model-facing calibration, not a security perimeter. Read middleware and tool exclusions separately.

  1. Filter middleware around replacements. Apply exclusions before and after caller replacement so excluded defaults cannot be resurrected accidentally. Classes match exact concrete types; strings match .name. Reject private underscore names, unsupported class-path grammar, and protected scaffolding: FilesystemMiddleware and SubAgentMiddleware cannot be removed this way.
  2. Validate match coverage at the right scope. Reject exclusions matching nothing, including stale keys/typos. Main-profile matches accumulate across main and automatic GP stacks because an entry may exist in only one. Independently profiled declarative children validate separately; compiled/remote children retain owner-chosen behavior rather than being silently rewritten.
  3. Filter tools and reject stale calls. Last-running tool exclusions remove caller and middleware schemas and also reject excluded names at execution. A fabricated or stale call cannot bypass mere schema hiding. Nevertheless, profiles explicitly call this calibration, not a security surface.
  4. Enforce real capabilities elsewhere. Direct backend access, filesystem-capable shells, and opaque compiled children can operate outside parent schemas. For read-only operation, restrict backend/process/network permissions and expose the intended subset. Renaming tools, omitting prose, or adding “never edit files” to a suffix is not authorization.

sections.title: RubricMiddleware adds a bounded evaluate–revise loop
sections.body:
A rubric gives the agent explicit criteria to evaluate after drafting, such as “the report answers the brief and lists unresolved questions.” RubricMiddleware can turn grader feedback into another model turn. It is public and optional, not core-installed; invocation state containing a rubric activates a lazily built nested LangChain grader.

Illustrative draft → feedback → revision → cap

  1. Draft. The agent finishes a report. Grader evaluation 1 returns needs_revision because open questions are missing.
  2. Feedback. Middleware adds a labelled human revision message and jump_to="model". The agent can revise the report; this is another graph transition, not the grader editing the file.
  3. Revision. Evaluation 2 can return satisfied and stop. If it instead requests revision, another model turn is allowed.
  4. Cap. If evaluation 3 still requests revision under the default three-iteration cap, status becomes max_iterations_reached. The graph does not pretend the criteria passed or schedule an unlimited fourth attempt.

These outcomes are hypothetical, not observed grader verdicts. A consumer still needs to inspect final rubric status before treating a saved /notes/report.txt as accepted.

Reference: activation, reset, grading inputs, and terminal behavior
  • Bounded attempts. The default maximum is three grader iterations, validated as a positive non-boolean integer. A new rubric—or the same rubric after a terminal result—resets run ID, iteration count, status, and frozen criteria.
  • Natural-stop grading. The nested grader uses GraderResponse structured output and optional tools/middleware. needs_revision loops as above; other results terminate. Grader interrupts propagate as graph control flow, not grader_error.
  • Input and criteria limits. Payloads use nonce-bracketed rubric/transcript sections, sanitize delimiter-like text, and warn that transcripts are untrusted. Usable criterion names freeze after first reporting. Coverage problems can downgrade “satisfied,” but the initial criterion count is not independently parsed/validated. This is an LLM evaluation aid, not exhaustive requirement or security proof.
  • Consumer enforcement. Inspect final rubric status, callback, or stream event. Non-satisfied termination does not automatically replace the assistant's last answer with a truthful failure notice. Callbacks provide observability; ordinary callback exceptions log. A hard acceptance gate must inspect structured status in application logic.

Architectural seam: hooks add scoped state and change graph transitions without creating another runtime. They do not replace application correctness enforcement.

sections.title: A practical diagnosis checklist by execution boundary
sections.body:
Follow the earliest boundary capable of explaining the surprise. This is a diagnosis order, not a claim that every run emits the same events.

  1. Model construction and harness selection. Was input a string or an initialized object? Which provider kwargs/hooks ran? Did the original identity match an exact model or only provider fallback?
  2. Graph assembly and request projection. Did caller middleware replace by name, exclusions remove it, or an automatic GP child appear? Then inspect routing, skills disclosure, capability filtering, and summarization to see what actually reached the provider.
  3. Tool dispatch and backend effects. Inspect call ID, argument validation, permission decision, and registered capability: hidden is not unregistered. Check backend result and routing; an offload pointer helps only if its write succeeded and stays reachable.
  4. State merge and background ownership. Identify changed fields and reducers for parallel writes. Distinguish task ID from current run ID, child HITL pause from cancellation, and notification delivery from authoritative server state.

Illustrative middleware composition, not executed here:

from deepagents import create_deep_agent, FilesystemMiddleware
from langchain.agents.middleware import TodoListMiddleware

agent = create_deep_agent(
    model="openai:gpt-5.5",
    backend=backend,  # an initialized application-owned backend
    middleware=[
        FilesystemMiddleware(
            backend=backend,
            tools=["read_file", "ls", "glob", "grep"],
        ),
        TodoListMiddleware(),
    ],
)

This replaces the default filesystem slot and adds LangChain planning. It is not a complete sandbox: other tools, child graphs, backend credentials, and process access must match application policy.

Maintainability: use the narrow existing extension seam rather than copying the constructor into a diverging second harness.
